summary.text: A 49-year-old man was involuntarily admitted to a psychiatric hospital after a failed suicide attempt. Examination showed depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, loss of self-confidence, self-blame without delusional depth, persistent suicidal ideation, concentration problems, terminal insomnia and loss of appetite, most present for 3 weeks. No bipolar, recurrent depressive or personality disorder features were present.

Brain CT and laboratory tests including thyroid hormones, alcoholemia and urine toxicology were completely negative. He was diagnosed with first-episode depressive disorder with marital disharmony as a contributing factor. QEEG assessments were done on hospital days 2 and 9, and theta prefrontal cordance was reported as 0.33 before treatment and 0.43 after 7 days of therapy.

He received psychotherapy and sertraline 100 mg per day and responded with a reduction of more than 60% in MADRS total score. Suicide risk assessments with the C-SSRS and Rorschach test found no acute suicidal risk, and psychological examination described his suicidal behavior as demonstrative. He was discharged after 10 days of treatment.

An outpatient psychiatrist re-evaluated him 7 days after discharge and found no signs of acute suicidal risk or worsening of depressive symptoms. On the 10th day after discharge he died by suicide by jumping out of the window of his flat. The authors suspect he dissimulated his symptoms.
